title: UBCS 32-Bit Command Frame Architecture
description: The Universal Binary Bot Control System encodes every bot command as a fixed 32-bit frame: an 8-bit opcode (256 possible commands), a 4-bit bot-class field (void, light, plasma, portal and 12 reserved classes), and a.

overview: The whole system in one frame

The Universal Binary Bot Control System encodes every bot command as a fixed 32-bit frame: an 8-bit opcode (256 possible commands), a 4-bit bot-class field (void, light, plasma, portal and 12 reserved classes), and a 20-bit operand (about one million distinct values). Fixed-width frames mean the decoder is a few bit-shifts, the worst-case decode time is constant, and every frame is exactly 4 bytes on the wire. With 4 bot classes active, the class field selects the command dictionary; the opcode selects the action inside that dictionary; the operand carries the parameter.

sections.heading: Why fixed width
sections.body: Variable-length commands save bytes but cost decoder complexity and make worst-case timing hard to prove. A 32-bit fixed frame gives O(1) decode and a hard upper bound on bandwidth: at 1 Mbit/s the channel carries at most 31,250 frames per second, and that number is a ceiling you can plan around, not a hope.

sections.heading: Addressing
sections.body: Bot-class is not the node address. Node addressing is a separate 16-bit field carried in the operand for addressed commands, giving 65,536 nodes per swarm (2^16). Broadcast commands use operand 0xFFFFF as the all-nodes address.

demo.program:
# UBCS 32-bit command frame: [opcode:8][botclass:4][operand:20]
def encode(opcode, botclass, operand):
    assert 0 <= opcode <= 255 and 0 <= botclass <= 15 and 0 <= operand < 2**20
    frame = (opcode << 24) | (botclass << 20) | operand
    return format(frame, '032b')
def decode(bits):
    frame = int(bits, 2)
    return (frame >> 24) & 0xFF, (frame >> 20) & 0xF, frame & 0xFFFFF
op, bc, val = 58, 1, 70001
bits = encode(op, bc, val)
d = decode(bits)
print("frame :", bits)
print("opcode:", d[0], "| botclass:", d[1], "| operand:", d[2])
assert d == (op, bc, val), "round-trip failed"
print("round-trip OK: encode -> decode is lossless")
demo.expected_output:
frame : 00111010000100010001000101110001
opcode: 58 | botclass: 1 | operand: 70001
round-trip OK: encode -> decode is lossless

title: UBCS Opcode Table: 256 Commands Across Four Bot Classes
t: UBCS Opcode Table: 256 Commands Across Four Bot Classes
description: Opcodes 0x00-0x3F are shared system commands (halt, reset, report status, acknowledge, heartbeat) understood by every bot class. Opcodes 0x40-0xFF are class-specific: the same byte means different things per class,.

overview: One table, four dialects

Opcodes 0x00-0x3F are shared system commands (halt, reset, report status, acknowledge, heartbeat) understood by every bot class. Opcodes 0x40-0xFF are class-specific: the same byte means different things per class, selected by the 4-bit class field. This gives 64 shared plus 192 class-specific commands per class, 832 distinct command meanings total across the four classes, from one byte of opcode.

sections.heading: Shared range (0x00-0x3F)
sections.body: 0x00 NOP, 0x01 HALT, 0x02 RESET, 0x03 STATUS_REQUEST, 0x04 ACK, 0x05 HEARTBEAT, 0x06 SELF_TEST, 0x07 REPORT_POSITION, 0x08 ENTER_SAFE_MODE, 0x09 RESUME. Every bot implements all of these; a STATUS_REQUEST must be answered within 50 ms.

sections.heading: Class ranges (0x40-0xFF)
sections.body: Voidbot: vacuum/pressure actuation verbs. Lightbot: photonic routing verbs. Plasmabot: RF plasma actuation verbs. Portal-bot: bridge/traversal verbs defined as a control protocol for hypothetical spacetime actuation hardware. Reserved classes return NACK for any class opcode.

title: Bot-Class and Node Addressing: 65,536 Nodes Per Swarm
t: Bot-Class and Node Addressing: 65,536 Nodes Per Swarm
description: The 4-bit class field picks the command dictionary; a 16-bit node address carried in addressed commands picks the bot. 2^16 = 65,536 addressable nodes per swarm, per class, so one swarm can hold up to 262,144 bots.

overview: Two-level addressing

The 4-bit class field picks the command dictionary; a 16-bit node address carried in addressed commands picks the bot. 2^16 = 65,536 addressable nodes per swarm, per class, so one swarm can hold up to 262,144 bots across the four classes. Address 0x0000 is reserved (unassigned), 0xFFFF is the class broadcast address.

sections.heading: Why 16 bits
sections.body: Sixteen bits fit comfortably in the 20-bit operand with 4 bits left for flags. Larger swarms are built by federating swarms: a 4-bit swarm ID prefixes the node address at the network layer, giving 16 swarms of 65,536 nodes each without changing the frame format.

title: CRC-32 Command Integrity Verification
description: Each 32-bit command frame is followed by a 32-bit CRC (IEEE 802.3 polynomial 0x04C11DB7). The receiver recomputes the CRC over the frame and drops any frame whose checksum mismatches, then requests retransmission..

overview: Every frame is checksummed

Each 32-bit command frame is followed by a 32-bit CRC (IEEE 802.3 polynomial 0x04C11DB7). The receiver recomputes the CRC over the frame and drops any frame whose checksum mismatches, then requests retransmission. CRC-32 detects all single-bit and double-bit errors, all odd-count bit errors, and all burst errors up to 32 bits long. For random corruption the undetected-error probability is about 2^-32, roughly one in four billion.

sections.heading: Cost
sections.body: CRC-32 doubles the per-command wire cost from 4 to 8 bytes. At 1 Mbit/s the usable command rate with CRC becomes about 15,625 commands per second. That is the honest price of integrity, and the system pays it on every frame.

demo.program:
import binascii
frame = bytes([0x3A, 0x21, 0x07, 0xFF])  # one 32-bit UBCS command frame
crc = binascii.crc32(frame) & 0xFFFFFFFF
print("frame bytes:", frame.hex(), " CRC-32: %08X" % crc)
# flip one bit and show detection
bad = bytearray(frame); bad[2] ^= 0x01
crc2 = binascii.crc32(bytes(bad)) & 0xFFFFFFFF
print("bit-flip detected:", crc2 != crc, "(%08X != %08X)" % (crc2, crc))
assert crc2 != crc
print("integrity check works: any single-bit error is caught")
demo.expected_output:
frame bytes: 3a2107ff  CRC-32: E51E9244
bit-flip detected: True (FC05A305 != E51E9244)
integrity check works: any single-bit error is caught

title: Supervisory Optical Override Channel
description: Commands tagged priority 0 travel on the supervisory channel and preempt every lower-priority command in every bot's queue. In the reference design the supervisory channel is optical: a free-space or fiber light link.

overview: Priority-0 preemption

Commands tagged priority 0 travel on the supervisory channel and preempt every lower-priority command in every bot's queue. In the reference design the supervisory channel is optical: a free-space or fiber light link that is physically separate from the RF command link, so a jammed or saturated RF link cannot block a stop command. Two priority-0 commands exist: OVERRIDE_HOLD (freeze in place) and OVERRIDE_SAFE_MODE (drop to minimum-energy safe state).

sections.heading: Engineering, not magic
sections.body: This is ordinary supervisory control: a separate, higher-priority channel with a simpler protocol. Any bot class can be fitted with the optical receiver; in the reference four-class system the lightbot class carries the optical transmitters, which is why supervisory authority is associated with it. The authority comes from the channel priority in software, and it can be audited: every override is logged with timestamp and operator key.

demo.program:
# Supervisory override: priority-0 optical channel preempts lower priorities
import heapq
cmds = [("routine sweep", 3), ("thermal adjust", 2), ("OVERRIDE: hold position", 0),
        ("formation keep", 3), ("OVERRIDE: safe mode", 0)]
q = []
for i, (name, pri) in enumerate(cmds):
    heapq.heappush(q, (pri, i, name))
order = [heapq.heappop(q)[2] for _ in range(len(q))]
print("execution order:")
for c in order: print("  ", c)
assert order[0].startswith("OVERRIDE") and order[1].startswith("OVERRIDE")
print("priority-0 supervisory commands preempt all others: OK")

title: Swarm Consensus Protocol (2f+1 Quorum)
description: When a swarm must agree on one action (advance, halt, split formation), each bot broadcasts its vote and the action with a strict majority of all n nodes wins. With n >= 2f+1 nodes the swarm reaches the correct decision.

overview: Agreement under faults

When a swarm must agree on one action (advance, halt, split formation), each bot broadcasts its vote and the action with a strict majority of all n nodes wins. With n >= 2f+1 nodes the swarm reaches the correct decision even if f nodes are faulty or malicious, because the faulty votes can never form a majority on their own. This is the standard quorum result, not a new invention.

sections.heading: Numbers
sections.body: A 7-node cell tolerates 2 faulty nodes. A 25-node swarm tolerates 12. Voting runs in two rounds (propose, commit); each round is one broadcast per node, so consensus costs 2n messages.

demo.program:
# Swarm consensus: 2f+1 nodes tolerate f faulty nodes (standard quorum math)
n, f = 7, 2
assert n >= 2 * f + 1, "quorum too small"
votes = ["ADVANCE"] * (n - f) + ["HALT"] * f   # f faulty nodes vote wrong
from collections import Counter
winner, count = Counter(votes).most_common(1)[0]
quorum = n // 2 + 1
print(f"nodes={n} faulty={f} quorum={quorum} winner={winner} votes={count}")
assert count >= quorum
print("consensus reached despite", f, "faulty node(s)")

title: Command Throughput Model
description: Throughput in commands per second equals channel bit rate divided by bits per command, minus protocol overhead. A 1 Mbit/s link carrying 32-bit frames plus 32-bit CRCs (64 bits per command) delivers at most 15,625.

overview: Bandwidth is the ceiling

Throughput in commands per second equals channel bit rate divided by bits per command, minus protocol overhead. A 1 Mbit/s link carrying 32-bit frames plus 32-bit CRCs (64 bits per command) delivers at most 15,625 verified commands per second; with 20 percent framing and retransmission overhead the sustained usable rate is about 12,500 commands per second. These are ceilings from division, not aspirations.

sections.heading: Scaling
sections.body: Throughput scales linearly with channels: four parallel 1 Mbit/s links give about 50,000 verified commands per second. There is no infinite filtering; every filter stage is a finite queue with a measured service rate, and the model says exactly what that rate is.

demo.program:
# Standard throughput math: frames/sec = channel_bps / frame_bits, minus overhead
ch, fb, oh = 1000000, 64, 0.2
raw = ch / fb
usable = raw * (1 - oh)
print(f"channel   : {ch:,} bit/s")
print(f"frame     : {fb} bits")
print(f"raw max   : {raw:,.0f} commands/s")
print(f"overhead  : {oh*100:.0f}% -> usable {usable:,.0f} commands/s")
assert usable < raw and usable > 0
print("throughput model checks out")

title: Latency Budget for Closed-Loop Bot Control
t: Latency Budget for Closed-Loop Bot Control
description: A closed control loop (sense, decide, command, actuate) must complete inside its deadline or the bot is flying blind. The reference budget: 20 ms sensing, 10 ms decision, 30 ms command transmission (one 64-bit verified.

overview: The 100 ms loop

A closed control loop (sense, decide, command, actuate) must complete inside its deadline or the bot is flying blind. The reference budget: 20 ms sensing, 10 ms decision, 30 ms command transmission (one 64-bit verified frame at 1 Mbit/s takes 0.064 ms; 30 ms covers queuing and retries), 40 ms actuation. Total 100 ms, i.e. a 10 Hz control loop. Faster loops need faster links or shorter frames; the arithmetic is shown, not assumed.

sections.heading: Jitter
sections.body: Worst-case jitter is bounded by the retransmission policy: at most 2 retries, each adding one frame time plus a 5 ms backoff, so worst-case command latency is 30 + 2 x 5.064 = 40.1 ms.

title: Voidbot Command Set: Vacuum and Pressure Actuation
t: Voidbot Command Set: Vacuum and Pressure Actuation
description: Voidbot class opcodes drive vacuum-state hardware: pumps, pressure regulators, and sealed-chamber actuators. 0x40 SET_PRESSURE takes a 20-bit operand mapped linearly to 0-101.325 kPa (about 0.0965 Pa per step). 0x41.

overview: What the commands mean

Voidbot class opcodes drive vacuum-state hardware: pumps, pressure regulators, and sealed-chamber actuators. 0x40 SET_PRESSURE takes a 20-bit operand mapped linearly to 0-101.325 kPa (about 0.0965 Pa per step). 0x41 VENT, 0x42 SEAL_CHAMBER, 0x43 PUMP_CYCLE. sections.heading: Frictionless propulsion note

Lightbot class opcodes drive photonic hardware: laser diodes, optical switches, and modulators. 0x40 SET_WAVELENGTH maps the operand to 400-700 nm (about 0.0003 nm per step, finer than any real tunable laser, so the driver quantizes to the device's actual resolution). 0x41 ROUTE_BEAM, 0x42 MODULATE, 0x43 HOLOGRAM_FRAME. overview: A protocol for hypothetical hardware

Portal-bot class opcodes define a control protocol for spacetime-bridge actuation hardware that does not exist yet: 0x40 OPEN_BRIDGE, 0x41 SET_ENDPOINT, 0x42 STABILIZE, 0x43 CLOSE_BRIDGE. title: Multi-Layer Swarm Task Distribution
description: Layer 1 (mission): the operator's goal, e.g. 'map this room'. Layer 2 (task): the goal split into tasks with dependencies. Layer 3 (assignment): tasks dealt to bot cells by capability and position. Layer 4 (execution):.

overview: Layers

title: Fault Detection and Failover
description: Every bot emits a heartbeat every 100 ms. If the controller misses 5 consecutive heartbeats (500 ms), the bot is declared failed: its tasks return to the assignment pool, a spare bot is tasked if one is free, and the.

overview: Heartbeat watchdogs

Every bot emits a heartbeat every 100 ms. If the controller misses 5 consecutive heartbeats (500 ms), the bot is declared failed: its tasks return to the assignment pool, a spare bot is tasked if one is free, and the failure is logged with the last known position and last acknowledged command. Detection time is bounded: between 500 and 600 ms, provable from the heartbeat period.

sections.heading: Failover
sections.body: Spare capacity is planned, not hoped for: swarms carry ceil(n/8) hot spares, so a 64-bot swarm carries 8 spares and survives 8 simultaneous failures without dropping tasks.

title: Binary Filter Pipeline (Finite, Measured)
description: Incoming command streams pass through filter stages: syntax check, authorization check, rate limiter, then dispatch. Each stage is a finite queue with a measured service rate; the pipeline's throughput is the minimum of.

overview: Filters are finite queues

Incoming command streams pass through filter stages: syntax check, authorization check, rate limiter, then dispatch. Each stage is a finite queue with a measured service rate; the pipeline's throughput is the minimum of the stage rates (the bottleneck), a standard result from queueing theory. There is no infinite filtering; there is a pipeline whose slowest stage is named and measured.

sections.heading: Backpressure
sections.body: When a stage's queue exceeds 80 percent of capacity, it signals backpressure and the upstream stage sheds the lowest-priority commands first. Shedding is logged, never silent.

title: Real-Time Command Scheduling (Rate-Monotonic)
description: Periodic command streams (sensor polls every 10 ms, actuator updates every 25 ms) are scheduled rate-monotonically: shorter period means higher priority. The Liu and Layland bound says n tasks are schedulable if total.

overview: Priorities from periods

Periodic command streams (sensor polls every 10 ms, actuator updates every 25 ms) are scheduled rate-monotonically: shorter period means higher priority. The Liu and Layland bound says n tasks are schedulable if total utilization is at most n(2^(1/n) - 1); for 4 tasks that is about 75.7 percent. The scheduler checks this bound at configuration time and refuses infeasible schedules loudly.

sections.heading: Aperiodic commands
sections.body: One-shot commands (like overrides) run on a sporadic server with reserved capacity, so they never break the periodic guarantees.

overview: Units in the operand

demo.program:
# UBCS 32-bit command frame: [opcode:8][botclass:4][operand:20]
def encode(opcode, botclass, operand):
    assert 0 <= opcode <= 255 and 0 <= botclass <= 15 and 0 <= operand < 2**20
    frame = (opcode << 24) | (botclass << 20) | operand
    return format(frame, '032b')
def decode(bits):
    frame = int(bits, 2)
    return (frame >> 24) & 0xFF, (frame >> 20) & 0xF, frame & 0xFFFFF
op, bc, val = 64, 2, 1048575

d = decode(bits)

print("opcode:", d[0], "| botclass:", d[1], "| operand:", d[2])
assert d == (op, bc, val), "round-trip failed"
print("round-trip OK: encode -> decode is lossless")

title: Manufacturing Blueprint Translation
description: A bot blueprint (parts list, tolerances, wiring map) is translated to machine instructions in three passes: 1) normalize the spec to the canonical schema; 2) expand each part to its fabrication operations; 3) emit the.

overview: From spec to machine instructions

A bot blueprint (parts list, tolerances, wiring map) is translated to machine instructions in three passes: 1) normalize the spec to the canonical schema; 2) expand each part to its fabrication operations; 3) emit the machine-specific instruction stream. Each pass is verified: the translator checks that every part in the spec produced operations and every operation traces to a part. Translation is deterministic: same spec plus same machine profile always yields the same program.

sections.heading: Verification, not faith
sections.body: The translator never trusts itself: an independent checker replays the instruction stream against the spec and reports any part with no covering operation.

title: Continuous Code Verification Loop
description: Deployed bots periodically re-verify: each bot recomputes the CRC of its loaded command set and compares it to the golden image hash held by the controller. Mismatch means corruption or tampering, and the bot drops to.

overview: Trust, but verify, forever

Deployed bots periodically re-verify: each bot recomputes the CRC of its loaded command set and compares it to the golden image hash held by the controller. Mismatch means corruption or tampering, and the bot drops to safe mode and requests a fresh image. Verification runs every 60 seconds and costs one hash computation; the loop is cheap because hashing is fast.

sections.heading: Perpetual optimization, honestly
sections.body: The controller profiles command timing and reorders each bot's dispatch queue so the hottest commands are checked first. 'Perpetual optimization' is this loop, measured in milliseconds saved, not a slogan.
